slides.title: Count the promises before counting the writes
slides.eyebrow: COUNT THE PROMISES BEFORE COUNTING THE WRITES
keyPoints: One item can fund one reservation
A decision and its update form one operation
Race conditions can exist with atomic variables
slides.narration: Two customers ask for the last available item. The requirement is simple: at most one request succeeds, and stock never becomes negative. Reading stock and later writing it back are not enough if another request can act between those steps. A race condition is a result that incorrectly depends on timing. A C++ data race is a narrower language rule about conflicting unsynchronized accesses, and it causes undefined behavior. The distinction matters because atomic accesses can remove the data race while leaving the reservation algorithm logically wrong. First state the whole promise, then choose an operation boundary that preserves it.

question.prompt: Can individually atomic reads and writes still sell one item twice?
question.answer: Yes. Two requests can both decide from the same old stock value unless the check and update are coordinated.

slides.title: An invariant is wider than a convenient statement
slides.eyebrow: AN INVARIANT IS WIDER THAN A CONVENIENT STATEMENT
keyPoints: Stock plus accepted reservations stays one
A failed reservation changes neither value
Every access path must obey the same rule
slides.narration: An invariant is a rule that must stay true when the state is visible to the next operation. Here, starting with one item, remaining stock plus accepted reservations should equal one. A reservation that fails must not consume stock. That relationship spans both a decision and a change. Locking only the final assignment would still allow two callers to make decisions from the same earlier value. A suitable critical section begins before checking availability and ends after the update is consistent. A suitable atomic operation instead combines the conditional replacement. Naming the invariant prevents a review from mistaking the mere presence of a mutex or atomic type for a complete solution.

slides.title: Safely model two stale reservation decisions
slides.eyebrow: SAFELY MODEL TWO STALE RESERVATION DECISIONS
keyPoints: Both requests read the one-item snapshot
Both accept from that same snapshot
The final stock hides the duplicate grant
slides.narration: This single-thread program deliberately models two separate requests reading the same stock snapshot. Each then stores snapshot minus one and marks its own grant. It prints remaining=0 grants=2 accounted=2. The remaining stock looks plausible, but the accounting invariant reveals the duplicated reservation. No actual concurrent ordinary access is executed, so this example has no C++ data race. Its purpose is to show a logical schedule with explicit steps. A test that checked only final stock would miss the defect. The repaired design must protect the decision as well as the store, so only one request can successfully consume that one unit.

slides.title: Run one indivisible claim on the last item
slides.eyebrow: RUN ONE INDIVISIBLE CLAIM ON THE LAST ITEM
keyPoints: CAS replaces one only if it is still one
Exactly one contender succeeds
Join before inspecting per-thread results
slides.narration: The repaired demonstration uses compare_exchange_strong to change stock from one to zero only if it is still one. Both workers begin with an expected value of one. One successful comparison consumes the item; the other observes that the value is no longer one and fails. Each writes its own result slot, and main reads those slots only after both joins. The output grants=1 remaining=0 is stable even though the winning thread is not predictable. This small one-shot protocol has only the states one and zero. A reusable inventory with replenishment would need a broader loop and lifetime contract rather than assuming this exact two-state proof still applies.

slides.title: Where the simple approach fails
slides.eyebrow: WORKSHOP · CONTRACTS AND EVIDENCE
keyPoints: Stronger memory ordering on separate load and store calls does not combine them into a transaction.
A related failure in the generalized operation is concrete: Replace fetch_add with load followed by store in each worker. The C++ accesses remain atomic, but increments can be lost.

The repair changes the operation at the point where the rule can be enforced: Use one read-modify-write operation for the counter, or protect the entire logical update with a mutex when several objects must change together.

slides.title: Mechanism, guarantees, and limits
slides.eyebrow: WORKSHOP · CONTRACTS AND EVIDENCE
keyPoints: Every access to each shared atomic counter is atomic, but only fetch_add combines reading and updating into one indivisible operation. The split trace intentionally separates those steps and has a logical lost update without undefined behavior. Completion of both futures makes the final count meaningful; checking while workers run would observe a valid but incomplete total.
A plausible alternative: Use a mutex when one logical update must protect several related values; one atomic counter is enough only for the narrower contract.

slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: Shared state is information accessible to multiple activities.
Mutable shared state requires a policy: one owner, a lock, atomic operations, or another proven protocol.
The policy should cover related fields together when their relationship forms an invariant.
A common design improvement is to reduce sharing.

Two ordinary reads can coexist when the object is safely initialized and remains alive. Different source-level variables can still interact through aliasing or overlapping storage. Conversely, distinct non-bit-field array elements are separate memory locations for ordinary concurrent-access reasoning. Hardware cache-line sharing is a performance concern distinct from language-level location identity.

slides.title: Race conditions
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: A check-then-act sequence can race even when each individual check and update is atomic.
Two customers may both observe the last item as available and each reserve it unless the combined transaction is coordinated.
Define the intended indivisible operation.
Is it one counter increment, a transfer between two accounts, or removal of one queue item together with count adjustment?

slides.title: Data races
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: In C++, conflicting accesses in different threads require the appropriate happens-before relationship unless the accesses are covered by the atomic rules.
A non-atomic shared counter increment without synchronization is not merely allowed to lose updates; the program has undefined behavior.
Do not use a run that “usually prints the expected number” as evidence of correctness.
Compiler transformations and hardware execution are constrained by the language’s defined programs, not by a programmer’s preferred interleaving of an undefined one.

slides.title: Atomicity
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: Atomicity means that an operation is indivisible with respect to the relevant observers and model.
An atomic load and an atomic store are individually indivisible, but the pair is not automatically one atomic read-modify-write transaction.
Atomicity also has scope.
An atomic integer operation does not make a neighboring ordinary structure update safe.
slides.narration:
Atomicity means that an operation is indivisible with respect to the relevant observers and model. An atomic load and an atomic store are individually indivisible, but the pair is not automatically one atomic read-modify-write transaction. Atomicity also has scope. An atomic integer operation does not make a neighboring ordinary structure update safe. A transaction spanning several objects generally needs a broader synchronization protocol or carefully designed multi-object algorithm.

In plain English: This is a coordination rule that helps multiple workers share information without stepping on each other's work.

slides.title: Critical sections
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: A critical section is code that accesses state under an exclusion or coordination rule.
Its boundaries should preserve the state invariant: acquire the protection, inspect and update related fields, restore a consistent state, then release.
Keep blocking I/O and unknown callbacks outside a lock when possible, but do not shorten the section by moving required validation outside and reintroducing a race.
Performance changes must preserve the same indivisible logical operation.

Its boundaries should preserve the state invariant: acquire the protection, inspect and update related fields, restore a consistent state, then release. Keep blocking I/O and unknown callbacks outside a lock when possible, but do not shorten the section by moving required validation outside and reintroducing a race. Performance changes must preserve the same indivisible logical operation.

slides.title: A data-race-free lost update
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: The first phase below deliberately separates atomic load and store.
A barrier ensures that both participants read zero before either stores one.
The second phase uses fetch_add , which performs one atomic read-modify-write per increment.
Companion listing: ch45/logical_race.cpp
slides.narration:
The first phase below deliberately separates atomic load and store. A barrier ensures that both participants read zero before either stores one. The second phase uses fetch_add , which performs one atomic read-modify-write per increment. Companion listing: ch45/logical_race.cpp The expected output is load/store=1 fetch_add=2 . Every counter access is atomic, so the first phase has no C++ data race. It is still the wrong implementation of “count two increments.” Strong default memory ordering does not combine separate operations into a transaction. The barrier makes the failure deterministic and inspectable. This is preferable to a demonstration that runs undefined code repeatedly and hopes to display a surprising number.

slides.title: Do not teach undefined behavior as a fixed schedule
slides.eyebrow: DO NOT TEACH UNDEFINED BEHAVIOR AS A FIXED SCHEDULE
keyPoints: Ordinary shared increments can be undefined
Models need explicitly defined steps
Atomic models preserve language correctness
slides.narration: The historical source includes a read-add-write explanation of counter increments. Use that explanation as a logical model, not as the promised outcome of racing ordinary C++ code. Two unsynchronized threads modifying the same non-atomic integer have a data race and therefore undefined behavior. The language does not promise only the numbers one or two. A safe lesson can serialize the modeled steps, as our reservation example does, or use atomic operations with a barrier to force a particular logical failure. That lets students observe a real, repeatable result while keeping the important distinction between algorithmic atomicity and the language's defined execution rules.

slides.title: Location identity and aliasing matter
slides.eyebrow: LOCATION IDENTITY AND ALIASING MATTER
keyPoints: Different names can reach the same storage
Distinct array elements can be independently written
Cache lines concern performance, not this identity rule
slides.narration: Suppose one function receives a pointer called left and another receives a pointer called right. The names do not prove independence; both pointers may designate the same integer. Race analysis follows actual overlapping storage and lifetime, not variable spelling. Conversely, our two ordinary result array elements are separate locations, and each worker owns one until joining. They may share a hardware cache line, which can affect performance, but that is distinct from a language data race. Review aliases, references, and returned pointers whenever ownership seems unclear. Destroying or reallocating shared storage can create a conflict even when the source code appears to contain only a harmless read.

slides.title: A mutex must protect the semantic transaction
slides.eyebrow: A MUTEX MUST PROTECT THE SEMANTIC TRANSACTION
keyPoints: Validate and update under one policy
Do not unlock between the check and commit
Keep callbacks outside unless their effects are included
slides.narration: A mutex repair is often clearer when a reservation changes several fields, such as stock, a customer record, and an audit sequence. The critical section should protect the semantic transaction, meaning the operation that observers must treat as one consistent change. Moving the availability check outside to shorten lock time reopens the stale-decision bug. On the other hand, calling unknown callbacks while locked can introduce reentry or deadlock. One solution is to update protected state, copy the notification data, release the lock, then call external code under a documented policy. The correct boundary follows the invariant, not a general rule that shorter or longer locking is always better.

slides.title: Testing needs both observations and a proof
slides.eyebrow: TESTING NEEDS BOTH OBSERVATIONS AND A PROOF
keyPoints: Stress tests explore some schedules
Race detectors find observed conflicts
Neither proves every logical invariant
slides.narration: Run a race detector to find conflicting accesses that a test actually exercises, but do not treat a clean report as proof that reservations cannot be duplicated. Our first model has a logical bug without any concurrent accesses at all. Useful tests count accepted requests, remaining stock, and unique item identities, then check the conservation rule after all work finishes. Forced schedules or barriers can expose known risky windows deterministically. The design argument explains why the repair excludes those windows. Tools and tests provide evidence about exercised paths; the invariant and synchronization rules explain why a wider set of permitted executions should remain correct.

slides.narration: Not every counting task needs a contended global atomic. Workers can count their own completed items and return totals for a parent to combine after joining. That changes the design so no two workers update the same counter. Reservation is different: deciding who receives the last item really does coordinate shared ownership, so independent local counts cannot replace the claim protocol. Distinguish statistics from allocation of a limited resource. A local count may be sufficient for reporting progress, while a global admission decision needs stronger coordination. Reducing sharing is often the simplest repair, but it must preserve the actual meaning of the operation.
